title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A graduate student and her professor discuss a research project on election administration.

script.en: Professor, do you have a minute? I'm working on my term paper about how state election boards interact with outside advocacy groups, and I've hit a wall.
Sure, come in. What's the problem? You've chosen a timely topic—there's been a lot of reporting on it lately.
That's just it. I found plenty of news articles, but they mostly describe what happened. I need scholarly analysis of whether these relationships compromise the independence of election officials.
Ah, you want to move from description to evaluation. That's the right instinct. Have you looked at the public administration literature on regulatory capture?
I've seen the term, but I assumed it applied mainly to industries like banking or utilities. Does it work for election boards too?

The core idea is adaptable. When an agency is supposed to oversee a process but develops close ties with a group it regulates, its decisions may start reflecting that group's preferences rather than the public interest. The key is to look for evidence of influence—not just meetings, but outcomes.
So I should trace whether the board's decisions changed after those meetings? Like, did they adopt tools or policies the group advocated?

Exactly. But be careful about causation. A correlation between meetings and policy shifts doesn't prove the group caused the shift. You'd need to rule out other explanations—public pressure, legal requirements, internal staff preferences.
That sounds like a lot of work. Is it feasible for a ten-page paper?

You don't need to prove causation definitively. You can present a plausible case and acknowledge limitations. Focus on one or two concrete decisions and examine the timeline and documented communications.
Okay. One more thing—should I interview people involved? I'm worried they won't talk to a student.
It's worth trying, but don't rely on it. Official records and recordings may be more reliable anyway. And remember, your paper should evaluate, not advocate. Keep the tone analytical.
Got it. I'll revise my outline to focus on two decisions and add a section on alternative explanations. Thanks—this really helps.
Good. Send me the revised outline by Friday, and we can talk again before you start writing.

script.en: In recent years, state election boards across the United States have found themselves under scrutiny for their ties to outside advocacy groups. These boards are typically expected to operate independently, ensuring that elections are administered fairly and without partisan interference. However, reports from several states suggest that some board members and staff have developed close relationships with organizations that promote specific views on election integrity. Such relationships are not inherently improper. Election officials often meet with community groups, civil rights organizations, and political parties to gather input and build public trust. The concern arises when these interactions begin to shape official decisions in ways that favor the agenda of a particular group. Experts in public administration refer to this phenomenon as regulatory capture, where an agency meant to oversee a process becomes aligned with the interests it is supposed to regulate. One area where this risk is particularly visible is the use of software tools to verify voter rolls. Some advocacy groups have pushed for the adoption of certain programs that flag potentially ineligible voters. While such tools can help maintain accurate lists, they are also prone to error and may disproportionately affect minority communities. When election boards adopt these tools at the urging of outside groups without thorough independent evaluation, questions arise about whose interests are being served. Defenders of the current arrangements argue that collaboration with advocacy groups brings valuable expertise and energy. They note that election officials are public servants who welcome input from engaged citizens. also, they point out that board members are appointed through a political process, so some degree of political alignment is unavoidable. Still, the line between productive collaboration and undue influence can be thin. Transparency is often proposed as a safeguard: requiring boards to disclose meetings with outside groups and the origins of policy proposals. in the end, public confidence in elections depends on the perception that decisions are made for the common good, not for the benefit of any single faction.

sections.title: Election Boards and Outside Influence
sections.passage: In the months before the midterms, Georgia's State Election Board and much of its staff reportedly coordinated with an activist network led by a conservative attorney who had challenged the 2020 outcome. Recordings reviewed by journalists show current and former board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allies on shared priorities, including promoting a controversial, error-prone software tool to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters. The board's vice chair and her predecessor both attended meetings of the network or an aligned group with overlapping membership and goals. The predecessor retired in June but remains active behind the scenes. At a fundraiser, the network's leader praised both officials, saying they had worked very hard together. At least three of the board's eight professional staff have attended network meetings, including those handling voter-fraud allegations and misconduct by election officials. The executive director has also worked closely with network members, sources say. Experts say these ties give the network extraordinary influence over how Georgia runs elections. The group has enlisted the board's help in getting counties to remove voters based on the software's information. A director at a voting advocacy nonprofit tracking the board said allies had captured it to sustain stolen-election claims and tilt Georgia toward one party, with the network as the behind-the-scenes driver. The board's leader said the more he looked, the more he realized the network had undue influence, which needed to cease. In response, a network leader urged followers on social media to inundate board members with messages defending the executive director and associated staffers. He warned that members might vote to terminate the executive director, investigators or staff, destroying the board as known, and said staff had made remarkable progress on election-corruption accountability and deserved raises, not termination threats. In interviews, the predecessor did not directly answer questions about her network ties. She said she was all about election integrity, wherever it came from, and acknowledged remaining involved after retirement because it gets in your blood. Two days later, she posted that the network's leader had the right ideas about running elections. The vice chair acknowledged discussing election matters with activists but said they did not influence her decisions. She saw no problem with network activists working for the board, though staff should be independent and nonpartisan; if they join organizations in private time, that is their choice. Told of staffers advancing network goals officially, she said she was unaware and it was the first she had heard. The network's leader did not respond directly but, after detailed inquiries, posted on social media celebrating the network's work with the election board. An election integrity group is working with election officials to oversee elections, the post read. Wow! What a discovery! Pulitzer anyone?

long_sentences.en: “EIN was the behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.” “The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into specifics about personnel matters.

In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.

“Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen 2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions.
